passage_text: Researchers at the Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory examined how different auditory cues influence reaction time in a simple go/no-go task. Twenty-four adult volunteers were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: (1) no auditory cue (control), (2) a low-frequency tone (200 Hz), (3) a high-frequency tone (2000 Hz), or (4) a broadband noise burst. Each participant completed 120 trials, with reaction times recorded for correct go responses. Table 1 summarizes the mean reaction times and standard deviations for each group. The investigators hypothesized that the high-frequency tone would produce the fastest responses due to its salience, while the broadband noise would have the least effect. Statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA) revealed a significant main effect of condition (F(3,20)=3.63, p=0.031). Post-hoc pairwise t-tests using the pooled error term indicated that the high-frequency group was significantly faster than the control (p=0.005) and the broadband group (p=0.024), but not significantly different from the low-frequency group (p=0.096). The authors concluded that frequency-specific auditory cues can modulate attentional readiness, with the high-frequency tone providing the greatest facilitation.
table_data:
Group | Mean RT (ms) | SD (ms)
Control | 520 | 45
Low-Freq | 480 | 50
High-Freq | 430 | 48
Broadband | 500 | 55
stem: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time according to Table 1?
explanation: The High-Frequency group had a mean RT of 430 ms, the lowest among all groups.
trap: Confusing the highest mean (control, 520 ms) with the lowest; faster responses correspond to smaller reaction times.

stem: Which of the following best describes the study design used in this experiment?
explanation: Participants were randomly assigned to experimental conditions, making this a randomized controlled trial.
trap: Calling it observational because only behavior was measured; participants were randomly assigned to conditions by the investigators, which makes it experimental.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the study’s findings?

options.A: High-frequency tone significantly faster than control
options.B: Control group had a higher mean RT than the low-frequency group
options.C: Low-frequency tone significantly slower than high-frequency
options.D: High-frequency tone significantly faster than broadband

explanation: Correct: C) The low-frequency group was not significantly different from the high-frequency group (p = 0.096), so the statement is false. Why the others are wrong: A) The high-frequency group was significantly faster than control (p = 0.005). B) Control (520 ms) was slower than low-frequency (480 ms). D) The high-frequency group was significantly faster than broadband (p = 0.024).
trap: Assuming the 50 ms gap between low- and high-frequency tones must be significant; the post-hoc p value was 0.096, so the data do not support a significant difference.

stem: By what percentage was the high-frequency group's mean reaction time lower than the control group's?
explanation: Correct: B) (520 - 430)/520 x 100 = 17.3%, using the control mean as the denominator. Why the others are wrong: A) 9.6% is 50/520, the low-versus-high-frequency difference rather than the control-versus-high-frequency difference. C) 20.9% divides by 430, the wrong denominator. D) 90 is the difference in ms, not a percentage.
trap: Dividing the 90 ms difference by the high-frequency mean (430) gives 20.9%; the comparison baseline is the control mean (520).
